findings.title: Options object flips rejectOnClear default to true
findings.cause: When the constructor receives an options object, destructuring defaults rejectOnClear to true instead of the documented false default.
findings.impact: Calling pLimit({concurrency: 1}) makes clearQueue() reject queued promises with AbortError even though the README and type docs say rejectOnClear defaults to false. Existing users that clear a queue without awaiting every discarded task can see unexpected rejections or Promise.all failures after switching from numeric concurrency to the equivalent options object.
findings.evidence: index.js:4 initializes rejectOnClear to false, but index.js:6-8 overwrites the default to true for options objects. readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document rejectOnClear as a boolean with Default: false. A focused Node probe using pLimit({concurrency: 1}), one running task, one pending task, and clearQueue() observed the pending promise reject with {name: 'AbortError', message: 'This operation was aborted'} instead of remaining pending.

findings.title: rejectOnClear accepts falsy non-boolean values
findings.cause: The runtime type check is guarded by the value itself, so only truthy non-booleans are rejected.
findings.impact: Invalid options such as {rejectOnClear: 0} or an empty string are silently accepted. That contradicts the public runtime error path, README/type contract, and can mask caller configuration mistakes while changing clearQueue behavior based on JavaScript truthiness instead of a boolean option.
findings.evidence: index.js:12 uses `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so falsy non-booleans bypass validation. readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 state the option type is boolean. index.test-d.ts:29 expects a string rejectOnClear to be rejected at type level, but there is no runtime test for falsy non-booleans. A focused probe observed pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0}) did not throw.

findings.title: limit.map drops indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper wrapper passes the Array.from index only when the original iterable is an Array; all other Iterable inputs receive undefined as the index.
findings.impact: Set, Map iterator, generator, and array iterator users get an undefined second argument even though the API promises a numeric index for every iterable. Code that keys output, performs pagination, or preserves source positions through mapperFunction will produce wrong results for documented iterable inputs.
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-84 says mapperFunction receives the item value and its index and is equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)). index.d.ts:40-43 types mapperFunction's second argument as number. index.js:108-112 computes iterableIsArray and passes undefined for non-arrays. The existing tests at test.js:239-254 cover Set and array iterators but only use the value argument, so the regression is untested. A focused probe returned [undefined, undefined] for a Set mapper's index argument.

findings.title: limitFunction wrapper discards caller arguments
findings.cause: The returned wrapper no longer accepts ...arguments_ and invokes the original function with no arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on runtime arguments now receives undefined values while the TypeScript definition still advertises full argument forwarding. This breaks the named export for common per-call input use cases and can silently return wrong data while respecting the concurrency limit.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts:133-136 declares limitFunction returns (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>. readme.md:111-117 describes a reusable limited function. index.test-d.ts:24-28 type-checks a one-argument limited function call, but test.js:343-357 only covers a zero-argument runtime case. index.js:124 returns `() => limit(() => function_())`, dropping all provided arguments. A focused probe with limitFunction(async value => value) returned undefined for limited('kept').

findings.title: Infinity concurrency is rejected despite the unbounded-number contract
findings.cause: validateConcurrency now requires Number.isInteger(concurrency), which excludes Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY.
findings.impact: Callers can no longer pass Infinity to express an effectively unbounded limiter, even though the API accepts a number with minimum 1 and the error message says a number from 1 and up. This is a behavioral regression for users relying on Infinity to disable limiting through configuration.
findings.evidence: readme.md:37-44 describes concurrency as Type: number | object, Minimum: 1, without an upper bound. index.js:128 rejects Infinity because Number.isInteger(Infinity) is false. git diff for index.js shows the previous guard allowed `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`. A focused probe observed pLimit(Infinity) throwing TypeError: Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up.

I used m1nd as the first investigative layer, recovered the cold graph via ingest, then verified final findings with direct source reads and focused Node runtime probes. npm test could not run because this workspace lacks the xo executable, so the proof relies on node --check plus targeted behavior probes.
